name: THE MOULD MAN AND THE SEA BURGER (Comes with blue cheese)

recipe.history:
Blue cheese is one of civilization's most celebrated accidents, and both Roquefort and Gorgonzola carry origin stories that lean into this mythology with obvious pride. Roquefort — made from the raw milk of Lacaune sheep and aged in the limestone caves of Combalou near the village of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon in southern France — has a legend that a young shepherd abandoned his lunch of bread and ewe's milk cheese in a cave to follow a beautiful girl on the horizon, and returned months later to find his cheese transformed by the blue-green mold Penicillium roqueforti into something magnificent. Whether or not the shepherd existed, the cheese certainly does, and it has been documented since at least 1070 CE, making it one of the oldest continuously produced cheeses in the world. Gorgonzola, its Italian counterpart, originates from the town of Gorgonzola near Milan in Lombardy and is thought to have been first produced in the 9th or 10th century, made from the milk of cows that had been driven down from the Alpine pastures for the season. Both cheeses share the essential technique: the introduction of Penicillium mold cultures into the paste, followed by needling — piercing the cheese to allow oxygen in and encourage the mold to grow in the blue-green veins that define the style.

Blue cheese found its way to the American burger through the same trajectory as many European gastronomic imports: first through fine dining, then through steakhouse tradition, and finally through casualization. The wedge salad with blue cheese dressing was a fixture of American steakhouses from the 1950s onward, and the pairing of pungent blue cheese with beef was familiar to anyone who frequented those rooms. By the 1970s, blue cheese burgers appeared on pub and bar menus as a natural extension of that pairing — the same logic that put blue cheese on a steak applied to the grilled patty. The stuffed blue cheese burger — where a nugget of Gorgonzola or Roquefort is hidden inside the patty itself — became a particular American innovation, but the simpler presentation of melted or crumbled blue cheese draped over the top of the patty became the standard. The funky, creamy, intensely flavored cheese is one of the few toppings bold enough to stand up to beef without disappearing.

I had my first truly transformative blue cheese burger in a wood-paneled bar in Vermont, on a snowy Tuesday night when I had stopped to wait out a storm on the interstate. The bartender put it in front of me without ceremony — a thick patty, still steaming, with a thick plug of Roquefort that had half-melted and half-remained crumbled over the top, the sharp dairy funk mingling with the char of the crust. There was nothing else on the burger except a smear of Dijon and a few leaves of frisée and I remember thinking that sometimes the best cooking is the kind that does exactly one thing right and refuses to apologize for its ambition. I have ordered or made blue cheese burgers hundreds of times since, but that storm-night burger is the reference point everything else gets measured against.

Cooking a burger to medium rare is an act of respect for the animal that provided the beef. At 130–135°F, the muscle is tense but yielding, the fat is liquid and fragrant, and the entire interior of the patty is working in your favor — basting itself, carrying flavor, providing the textural contrast to the crust that makes a great burger great. Blue cheese in particular demands a medium rare patty: the boldness of the mold-ripened cheese, the tang and funk of the veined paste, needs something equally assertive beneath it. A well-done patty, gray and dry, would make Roquefort taste like it was wasted. The medium rare center — pink and glossy — is the canvas on which the blue cheese performs.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
170g (6 oz) Roquefort or Gorgonzola (or a blend), crumbled
3 large shallots, peeled and very thinly sliced into rings
4 leaves frisée or curly endive, torn
1 medium red onion, thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl. Mix on low with dough hook.
2. Add warm milk, warm water, egg, and butter. Mix on low until combined, then medium speed for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Cover and let rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
4. Divide into 4 portions, shape into balls, place on a lined sheet pan, flatten. Proof covered 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.
6. MAKE THE BLUE CHEESE AIOLI — Mash together mayonnaise, crumbled blue cheese, and sour cream with a fork until mostly smooth with some texture remaining.
7. Stir in lemon juice, Worcestershire, and black pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
8. MAKE THE CRISPY SHALLOTS — Soak shallot rings in buttermilk for 15 minutes.
9. Combine flour, salt, pepper, and cayenne in a shallow bowl. Lift shallot rings from buttermilk (let excess drip off) and toss in the seasoned flour.

10. Heat about ½ inch of neutral oil in a skillet over medium-high heat to 350°F (175°C). Fry shallots in batches, turning once, until golden and crisp, 2–3 minutes. Drain on paper towels. Season with salt.

11. PREPARE THE BLUE CHEESE TOPPING — In a small saucepan over low heat, gently warm the crumbled blue cheese with the heavy cream, stirring until it forms a loose, creamy sauce. Do not boil. Remove from heat.

12. FORM THE PATTIES — Divide beef into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Form into patties ¾-inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and onion powder just before cooking.
13. COOK THE PATTIES — Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil until smoking.
14. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once.
15. Cook 2–2½ more minutes. In the last minute, spoon or place a generous amount of blue cheese (crumbled or warm sauce) over each patty.
16. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
17. Remove and tent with foil. Rest 3 minutes.
18. TOAST THE BUNS — Split buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat, 60–90 seconds.
19. ASSEMBLE — Spread blue cheese aioli on both cut sides of the bun.
20. Place a few leaves of frisée on the bottom bun.
21. Add red onion rings.
22. Set the blue cheese-topped patty on the onions.
23. Pile crispy shallots over the blue cheese.
24. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
